supportMap.description: Hitchens says substitution can cover another person's cost but cannot remove that person's sins or responsibility for the act.
supportMap.anchor: what they can't do is take away your sins because that would be to take away your responsibility

supportMap.description: He allows that love can motivate paying another person's debt or voluntarily taking that person's prison sentence or execution.
He insists that payment cannot make the original theft, loss, or conduct leading to prison cease to have occurred.
supportMap.anchor: I can't say you didn't steal or lose that money

supportMap.description: He characterizes vicarious redemption as the primitive transfer of sins onto a scapegoat animal.
supportMap.anchor: vicarious Redemption is scapegoating it's throwing your sins onto an animal

supportMap.description: He says the purported offer cannot freely be refused because refusal brings the threatened consequence of eternal torture.
supportMap.anchor: that means an eternity of torture

supportMap.description: The promised erasure exceeds what substitution can accomplish, and the offer becomes coercive when refusal is punished by death or eternal torture.
supportMap.anchor: you refuse it on pain of death

boundaryJustification.startWhy: Event 2841 begins the debt-payment example needed to distinguish permissible substitution from the claimed removal of responsibility.
boundaryJustification.endWhy: Event 2892 completes the warning that the supposed offer of eternal love carries eternal torture for refusal.
boundaryJustification.removedPrefix: Events 2779-2840 are removed because they discuss inherited sickness, Marcion, the Old Testament, Jesus' historicity and the setup of human sacrifice before the debt analogy begins.
boundaryJustification.removedSuffix: Events 2893-2896 are removed because the North Korea, celestial dictatorship and slave-worship labels repeat the already complete coercion conclusion without adding a named reason.

supportMap.description: Dembski defines forgiveness as payment of a moral debt while affirming that God remembers who committed the act.
supportMap.anchor: of course you did it and God remembers that you did it

supportMap.description: He presents penal substitution as Christ paying the debt represented by another person paying, serving the sentence, or dying in one's place.
He says remembered responsibility is compatible with forgiveness because God no longer holds the paid debt against the offender.
supportMap.anchor: but he's not going to hold it against you

supportMap.description: He argues that deterministic atheism undermines responsibility because without free will a person lacks the ability to act differently.
supportMap.anchor: if you don't have free will you don't have responsibility

supportMap.description: He concedes discomfort with hell and with the exclusivity of Jesus as the only way.
supportMap.anchor: hell I'm not real comfortable with that

supportMap.description: He describes worldviews as package deals containing tensions and denies that atheism is entirely neat either.
supportMap.anchor: with World Views often we're stuck with packaged deals

supportMap.description: The responsibility objection therefore mistakes debt cancellation for denial of history, while Dembski accepts Christianity as a hopeful package with unresolved tensions.
supportMap.anchor: there there are tensions that we all deal with

boundaryJustification.startWhy: Event 2908 begins Dembski's direct identification of the disputed relation between sins and responsibility, immediately introducing his penal-substitution answer.
boundaryJustification.endWhy: Event 2972 completes his qualification that atheism also is not a neat worldview after acknowledging tensions in the Christian package.
boundaryJustification.removedPrefix: Events 2897-2907 are removed because they contain a speaking preface and a separate scriptural answer that humanity is already dead and is offered life, not the debt-versus-history reasoning summarized here.
boundaryJustification.removedSuffix: Events 2973-2976 are removed because the observation that debaters pretend to have everything settled repeats the already complete admission of worldview tensions.

repairs.longerCompleteArgumentRationale: The range must retain several separated parts: events 2908-2926 distinguish paid liability from remembered conduct; events 2927-2942 supply the free-will challenge to atheistic responsibility; and events 2947-2972 preserve the material concessions about hell, Christian exclusivity, packaged worldviews and unresolved tensions. The intervening events 2943-2946 connect the challenge to those concessions, so deleting them would stitch noncontiguous excerpts.
